query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The onset and progression of premelting and melting in FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by differential elemental segregation driven by local surface energy and melting point disparities. In particular, the lower-melting-point copper preferentially segregates to the particle surface upon heating, forming an initial liquid-like layer. This Cu-rich layer reduces the cohesive stability of the nanoparticle’s core and triggers subsequent bulk melting, while sub-surface regions enriched in elements with higher surface energy (Fe, Ni, Cr, Co) temporarily retard complete melting.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneously mixed, solid-solution FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles (initially single-phase, likely FCC)
generation.intervention: A controlled thermal ramp (heating experiment) conducted in an inert atmosphere with well-defined heating rates
generation.conditions: Experiments carried out under identical nanoparticle size distributions, inert environment to preclude oxidation, and heating rates that minimize macroscopic diffusion effects so that intrinsic atomic mobility governs surface segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of a surface composition gradient—specifically, a Cu-enriched, liquid-like surface layer juxtaposed with a relatively enriched sub-surface region in Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co—mediates the transition.
generation.mechanism: Upon heating into the premelting regime, copper (with its lower melting point) migrates to the surface due to its lower dissolution potential and surface energy, initiating a localized liquid layer. This phase demarcation undermines the cohesive energy of the nanoparticle core, progressively allowing the melting front to advance inward. The presence of higher-surface-energy elements beneath the surface delays complete melting until sufficient thermal energy is provided.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the homogeneous solid-state baseline, nanoparticles will first display a Cu-enriched, liquid-like surface layer at a temperature lower than the bulk melting point. High-resolution imaging and compositional mapping (e.g., in situ TEM/EDS) should reveal this surface segregation and the onset of melting initiating at the nanoparticle periphery, with delayed complete melting due to the stabilizing effect of the sub-surface enriched elements.
generation.baseline: Solid, homogeneously mixed FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles at room temperature with no pre-existing composition gradients.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected under controlled heating conditions with moderate heating rates and inert atmospheres. Under extremely rapid heating or oxidizing environments, alternate mechanisms (such as stress-induced melting or oxidation-driven phase changes) may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature shift due to Cu surface segregation, as well as the quantitative degree of elemental segregation and its impact on melting kinetics, remains to be precisely determined experimentally. The interplay between kinetic diffusion and thermodynamic driving forces may introduce complexities beyond this simplified model.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles: one in the as-synthesized, homogeneously mixed state and one with pre-induced surface enrichment of Cu (achieved via a surface treatment process). Expose both sets to a well-controlled thermal ramp in an in situ transmission electron microscope (TEM) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to monitor real-time structural and compositional changes.
measurements: In situ TEM imaging to track morphological changes and the appearance of a liquid-like surface layer
EDS mapping to quantify surface and sub-surface elemental compositions as a function of temperature
Determination of the onset temperature for the appearance of premelted regions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both nanoparticle sets exhibit the same onset temperature for surface premelting, or if no preferential Cu segregation is observed at the surface relative to the core under identical heating conditions, then the hypothesis that surface segregation (specifically of Cu) drives the melting progression is falsified.

The dissolution of a given particle was simulated by calculating the dissolution potentials of each surface atom depending on its local atomic environment, enabled by predicting the change in surface energy using a simple machine-learning regression model trained on density functional theory calculations. A stability parameter, measuring the number of (111) surface atoms before versus after the simulation, was presented to analyze stability trends in composition space through a grid search. Analyzing the stability composition space uncovered two stabilizing strategies through alloying: (1) Increasing the concentration of metals with reduction potential above the applied potential and (2) incorporating an element with a high relative surface energy. The dissolution model resulted in core–shell particles with shells depleted of elements with low dissolution potential in agreement with experimental studies on binary Pt-alloys. In effect, the dissolution proceeds until a stable layer forms, and its facilitation determines the size of the resulting particle.
